elements.text: The sound of wind blowing through an autumn forest. Several footfalls grow near, quick and rhythmic like trotting horses.
Then a burst of young female laughter.
A chilly, sunny afternoon along a dirt road. Late November. The trees, with what little leaves they still hold, create dappled light all over.
ROADSIDE. Tall weeds. A GRASS SNAKE pokes its head out. Feels the world with its tongue. It senses something, then disappears.
Suddenly, THREE GIRLS (pre-teens) gallop briskly up the road, their ponytails bouncing, legs trotting like horses.
The girls are riding HOBBYHORSES -- stuffed, fabric-wrapped horse heads fastened to the end of broomsticks.
The girls gallop up to a wooded trail that cuts into the forest. They stop at the trial’s entry.
One of the girls, KRISTA, 11, blonde and a bit chubby, fixes her attention to the dark wooded trail. She’s unsure.
BETH (12), tall, skinny, tomboyish, rolls her eyes at Krista.

elements.speaker: BETH
elements.text: It’s this way to the river, or else we go all the way around. For like an hour.
HOLLY (12), sweet face and very pretty, pats the neck of her hobbyhorse, a white Arabian stallion.

elements.speaker: HOLLY
elements.text: Our horses are thirsty, remember? We hafta get ‘em to water soon.
Krista runs her fingers through the black yarn of her hobbyhorse’s mane, gently, as if to comfort it.

elements.speaker: KRISTA
elements.text: Bella gets spooked on trails. She likes open spaces better.

elements.speaker: BETH
elements.text: Well, Bella’s gonna have to learn.
Holly produces an apple from her pocket. Gives it to Krista.
Krista takes the apple. She smiles. She role-plays feeding the apple to Bella.

elements.speaker: HOLLY
elements.text: Last one to the river mucks all our stalls for a week!
Holly suddenly breaks into a gallop down the wooded trail, leaving Beth and Krista in the dust.
Beth and Krista square their shoulders, grab their horse’s reins and stride off after Holly.
The girls racing playfully through the forest on their “horses”, hopping over logs and rocks.
Beth goes to pass Holly, but Holly easily out maneuvers her.
The girls giggle and squeal. Holly pulls away from Beth.
Holly, well ahead of the others now, gallops straight into...
A small clearing. Holly appears, pauses. Catches her breath. She looks around...
She’s actually entered into a cemetery. Historic. Puritan New England. Headstones from the 1600’s.
Holly glances back at the trail she left behind. She smiles mischievously.
Holly runs up to a mossy headstone and ducks behind it. She lets out a quiet laugh.
A moment... The wind blows. Fallen leaves spray across the cemetery.
Suddenly, a branch SNAPS, heavily on the other side of the cemetery. Holly spins and looks to the source, to the far side of the cemetery, into the dark forest.
Her mischief falls from her face, as we stay on her, unable to see the danger that she sees.
Holly turns back and peeks around the headstone at Beth and Krista arriving at the edge of the clearing.

elements.speaker: KRISTA
elements.text: Why does she always do this?

elements.speaker: BETH
elements.text: Cuz she’s weird. She’s probably already at the river. C’mon.
Beth and Krista trot off down the trail.
Watching her friends disappear. She looks back again at the far side of the cemetery... Nothing but trees now.
Finally, she gets up and gallops away -- not toward her friends, and not toward whatever she saw on the far side of the cemetery, but decidedly somewhere in between.
Muddy banks of the river. Tall grasses. Logs and rocks. The sun hangs low as tall, cold shadows cloak the riverbank.
Krista sits on a log, dabbing away a spot of river water from her horse’s mouth with her coat sleeve.
Further down shore, Beth tries to skip stones across the water. She gives up and walks over to Krista and sits down.

elements.speaker: BETH
elements.text: It’s been twenty minutes. I’m calling her.
Beth takes out her cell, begins to dial.

elements.speaker: KRISTA
elements.text: So, does this mean we win?

elements.speaker: BETH
elements.text: No. It means I win, moron. I got here first.
Krista frowns. Beth hangs up her phone, unable to reach Holly. She begins to tap out a text --

elements.speaker: BETH
elements.text: Where r-u you dumb... little... sh-
A SCREAM. A girl’s scream. Holly. Distant and cut-off suddenly as if by force.
The girls spin and look into the woods, chilled by the terror of the sound.
Ancient stone foundation overgrown with brush, grass. Once a house, now a remnant of New Hampshire’s earliest settlers.
Krista is here, standing at the edge of the foundation, full of fear and confusion. Beth runs up to her, out of breath.
Krista points at the foundation. Beth looks down at...
The foundation’s grassy floor, and laying there within it, squared off by the stones of over 350 years of early American history...
Small town Dover. The night lit up by a full moon shimmering the Cocheco River that cuts through the town.

elements.speaker: ADULT MALE
elements.text: Lemme get this straight: three of you’s went into the park, but only the two of ya’s came out?
Bungalow. Quiet sub-division. Two POLICE CARS parked out front. Inside the home all the lights are on.
Hear the sobs of Beth and Krista.

elements.speaker: BETH
elements.text: Dad! That’s all we know! She just... disappeared.

elements.speaker: KRISTA
elements.text: Then we heard her screaming. And then we found her horse.

elements.speaker: ADULT MALE
elements.text: How could she just vanish? She say she was going somewhere?

elements.speaker: BETH
elements.text: I don’t know where she is!
More sobs. And as we FADE TO BLACK...

elements.speaker: ADULT FEMALE
elements.text: Girls, just tell the officers what happened. Okay? Can you do that?

elements.speaker: ADULT MALE
elements.text: Wait. Has anyone called the mother?

slugline: EXT. GOOD TIMES TAVERN - LOS ANGELES - MORNING
location_time: GOOD TIMES TAVERN - LOS ANGELES - MORNING

elements.text: A dreary-looking tavern near the airport in Inglewood. Security bars guard the heavily tinted windows.
Not any less dreary inside. A few drunk unsavories at the bar, half-watching a college football game on the big-screen.
Cheap Thanksgiving decor has been placed around the bar -- images of cornucopias, cartoonish turkeys. It’s the effort that counts.
From somewhere in back sound the digital bleeps and melodies of a video poker machine.

DETECTIVE JOHN KIERSTEAD, 41, sits on a barstool, burning cigarette in his hand as he taps away at the cards on the screen. He’s lean and attractive, seems calm, but with eyes always tense, anticipating.
The machine sings as John wins a big hand. He barely reacts.
BARTENDER comes by with a shot of bourbon. He sets the shot down next to John.
John bets big again. Loses. Sighs. Looks over at the shot of bourbon for a long moment. He finally reaches for it just as--
His pager buzzes at his hip. He peeks down, studies it.
He springs off the stool and downs his shot and grabs his coat and heads for the door. He tosses a wad of wrinkled bills onto the bar on his way out.
John exits. Bartender picks up the bills, counts them out. He stops -- an angered expression of being short-changed.
Two-storey apartment complex on the corner. The circus is already here -- EMS. Fire. Uniformed cops and some news vans.
An unmarked rolls up and stops. John gets out of it. He fires up a cigarette. He casts a wide look across the scene.
A uniformed hurries past us with a roll of yellow crime tape. The ribbon unfurling behind him, tied to something unseen, separating John from the crime scene. John stops the officer.
The officer winds the tape around a sign pole, cordons off the area.

elements.speaker: OFFICER
elements.text: Two on the lawn, three more inside.
John glances over at the house.
On the grass-barren front lawn lay two dead bodies -- man and woman, 30’s, gunshots through the head. Blood all over. Two lawn chairs upended close by.

elements.speaker: OFFICER
elements.text: Like they never saw it comin’.
Visuals of the neighborhood: homeowners on their stoops, on- lookers in their cars. Everyone watches, on edge, but nobody talks.

elements.speaker: OFFICER
elements.text: Streets are blind as usual. Buncha

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: See no evil, hear no evil, and you will survive.
He dips under the tape and makes his way up to the house. Suddenly a hand grips his shoulder, stops him. John turns, sees--

elements.speaker: SARGE
elements.text: I already got a team in there.
SARGE, 50’s, large and in charge, keeps his hand on John’s shoulder as he leads him away from the crime scene.

elements.speaker: SARGE
elements.text: I need you to head out and canvass

elements.speaker: SARGE
elements.text: You got a problem with that?
John keeps his focus on the house behind Sarge where Coroners carry out a bodybag. A small one. Kid-sized.

elements.speaker: SARGE
elements.text: You took a few months off. You did what you had to do. And believe me when I say that everybody here is super proud of your decision.
John shifts his weight, impatient, and feeling patronized.

elements.speaker: SARGE
elements.text: But there is no way I’m letting you
Another detective walks by. DET. MCAVOY, Latino, very fat. He carries a tray of coffee and donuts for the team.

elements.speaker: DET. MCAVOY
elements.text: Welcome back, Kierstead. Little late to the party, huh? You avoid the liquor stores and take the long way around?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Nah, too busy turkey-basting your fat-ass whore of a mother.
Det. McAvoy flips John the finger.

elements.speaker: DET. MCAVOY
elements.text: Fuck you, Kierstead. You and your fucking attitude.

elements.speaker: DET. MCAVOY
elements.text: Yeah. I hope you fuckin’ relapse. You know that?
John whips out a mickey of whiskey from his coat pocket. Shakes it at McAvoy.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Way ahead of ya, ya fat fuck!
The two men begin shouting insults at each other. Sarge stops the dispute quickly and with AUTHORITY.
McAvoy, eyeing John, shakes his head and leaves.
John thrusts the finger at McAvoy.

elements.speaker: SARGE
elements.text: This is what I’m talking about.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: C’mon, you letting fat-ass McAvoy in there? Jesus, a fucking cream- puff’s more competent than him, and you know it! Just lemme inside. Lemme do my job.

elements.speaker: SARGE
elements.text: Not happening! You gotta work your way back up to that. That was the deal -- prove to us you deserve to be back in there. Until then, you’re door-to-door.
A woman’s WAIL behind Sarge breaks the moment. It’s the family. They’ve arrived on scene. The woman screams again, inconsolable grief. She collapses to the ground.
John behind the wheel of his unmarked. He turns down a residential road, pulls over, and shuts off his car.
He glances across the road at a shoddy ball field where a group of neighborhood boys play baseball. He sits and watches the boys play. A few moments pass. He gets out of his car.
John sparks a cigarette and starts to walk the beat. The crack of a baseball bat is heard. Well-hit ball. The boys all cheer, until...
CRASH! John pauses. Mid-smoke. He slowly turns...
Fuck. His car. Windshield obliterated by the homerun ball.
He glances across at the ball field. It’s empty. The chain- link gate at the field’s far end swings shut with a clank.
John walks a residential laneway, holding in his hand the baseball that broke his windshield.
CLOSE on: the BASEBALL, as John starts to turn it over in his hand, cycling through grips, pitch selections -- fastball, curveball, cutter. A nasty slider. Then a knuckleball grip.
His cycles are rapid and well-rehearsed, like he’s done them ten thousand times before.
A garage. Its door pulled almost shut. Almost. The heel of a baseball glove sits exposed under the door. A boy’s whisper:
The glove is quickly yanked back and disappears. More hushed voices as the boys begin to argue with each other.
John approaches the garage. Stops. The boys arguing stops. John throws open the garage door to...
THE BOYS. Half-dozen of them. Some of them look scared shitless. Others try to hide their shitless fear.
John has one hand gripping the baseball, the other on his hip pulling back his coat, showing a badge and gun. He holds up the ball.
Hesitation from the group. Then one of them, a BLACK KID, 12, big for his age, hardens up--

elements.speaker: BLACK KID
elements.text: Yeah. Can’t bust a kid for goin’ yard.
A shy, skinny LATINO KID, 11, doesn’t move, not a peep, eyes to the floor. The rest of the boys turn and look at him. Finally, the pitcher looks up and raises his hand, meekly.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: What do you guys know about that house down on East Olympic, by the 7-Eleven?

elements.speaker: BLACK KID
elements.text: Heard a whole family got iced.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: That’s right. Including a three year-old girl.
John checks their body language: at least one kid looks like he might know something. The pitcher. John senses it.
The boys look to one another, confused.
The boys and John walk onto the field.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Pitcher, come with me. Slugger, you’re up.
PITCHER’S MOUND John and the Latino Kid on the mound together. Black Kid steps up to the plate, eager, cocky.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Now, you’re a lefty. That’s a right- handed hitter. What pitch did you throw him when he crushed it into my windshield?

elements.speaker: LATINO KID
elements.text: I just threw it as hard as I could?
John hands the ball to the kid, and steps back.
John nods at Latino Kid, who throws the ball as hard as he can. Black Kid swings. CRACK! The ball soars, high and long and over the fence. Another mammoth dinger.
Latino Kid sighs, looks down, deflated. Black Kid grows more cocky. Bat flip. Spreads out his arms, puffs out his chest. Taunting--

elements.speaker: BLACK KID
elements.text: Big Papi! Big Papi! You can’t touch me! Chicks dig the long ball! Come and get it. You can’t touch me!
The ball is fetched, thrown back to John who steps back onto the mound with Latino Kid.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: How about I teach you a pitch that Mr. All-Star here won’t ever be able to hit?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Okay. But here’s the deal: I teach you this pitch, and if he can’t hit it, you tell me everything you know about that house down on Olympic. But if he does hit it, you don’t gotta say a word to me, and I walk away. Deal?
Latino Kid, wary, mulls this over. Finally, he nods ‘yes’.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Great. This time throw a changeup. Four-seamer. It’s gonna look like a fastball, but the speed will change, and it’ll throw his timing off and his balance off. And he won’t be able to hit it. Ever.
Latino Kid smiles at that possibility.
John demonstrates by palming the baseball across all four seams, tucking his thumb and pointer finger under the ball.
Tuck your thumb and finger together, like a circle.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: That’s it. Now, when you release the ball, keep your back leg solid, don’t be jumping off too much. This’ll control the speed of the pitch and it’ll fool him into thinking it’s a fastball.

elements.speaker: LATINO KID
elements.text: How hard do I throw it?
John steps off the mound. The kid gets into his stance. He grips the ball for the changeup. He winds up and releases the ball as hard as he can down the plate.
Black Kid swings mightily. Misses. Latino Kid, almost in disbelief, smiles back at John, who nods.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Nice pitch. Now do it again.
Ball is thrown back. Latino Kid repeats the grip, the stance. He releases the ball. Black Kid swings through it.
Once more: grip, stance, release. Strike three, he’s out. The rest of the boys clap and cheer. Black Kid stares down Latino Kid. He throws his bat and walks away frustrated.

elements.speaker: LATINO KID
elements.text: How’d you know how to do that?
John takes the ball. Studies it. A moment passes. He smiles.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: My dad taught me that pitch... long time ago.
John seems lost in “long time ago”. He snaps to.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: So what do you know ‘bout that house?

elements.speaker: LATINO KID
elements.text: I dunno shit, mister. The kid gives John a hard look and walks off the mound. John got played by a 12-year old. Damn.

slugline: EXT. LOS ANGELES - DAY TO NIGHT

elements.text: TIME LAPSE: the sun sets, night falls over the city.
John behind the wheel, looking tired.
John at the cash paying for cigs, snacks, and booze. John exits the store.
Young black woman, ANGIE, 20’s, in a skin-tight dress, stands outside a motel room door. A set of headlights sweep across her as John’s car pulls up, shuts off. John gets out.
John comes up to Angie, digs out some cash, peels off a few bills. She takes it and tucks it away in her purse. John unlocks the motel door, and the two step inside.
Sex. Angie is bent over the mini-bar as John gives it to her. Rough. The little bottles inside the fridge clank away.
The TV in the room is tuned to the Weather Network. A sexy weather woman announces a late November L.A. heat wave.
Angie off in the bathroom, cleaning herself up. John pours out two cups of whiskey.
Angie appears out of the bathroom, dressed to leave. John flashes her more money.

elements.speaker: ANGIE
elements.text: Still ain’t sleeping, huh? You know they got pills for that?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Just until the sun comes up?
Angie sitting by the TV tuned to a sitcom. She laughs at the show. She does a line of cocaine.
She takes a drink of John’s whiskey, looks across at John sound asleep in the bed. Snoring. Loudly.
Angie turns up the TV to drown out John. She does more coke. She laughs at the TV.
Morning. John’s cell phone on the night stand. It buzzes. Call display: TRUDY.
John stirs, wakes up. He looks at his phone. He answers it.
Door swings opens. A concerned-looking John steps out. It’s dawn and already the L.A. freeway is heavy with traffic.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Well, how did it happen..? Oh... Ok... yeah. But what am I--
Trudy on the other line. Heavy sobs. We hear her pleas--
A TAXI pulls up. Driver honks the horn.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I mean what am I supposed to... Look, if I can get time off work, then yes--

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I know! Fuck. Okay. Jesus Christ, Trudy.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I wouldn’t be able to stay long. A couple days at the most.
More honking. Angie steps out, ready to go. John, upset, hangs up the phone. Angie looks to him.

elements.speaker: ANGIE
elements.text: Oh... bummer. Well, I mean... that sucks.
She grows uncomfortable. Compassion isn’t her strong suit.

elements.speaker: ANGIE
elements.text: Hey. I’ll see you around, okay?
John doesn’t respond. Angie departs into the taxi. The taxi pulls away, leaving John alone, staring off into the freeway traffic.
The loud BUZZ of turbo prop engines. POV of a small window. Through it stretches an expanse of hilly New England countryside. Its endless trees explode with autumn colors.
John is seated at the window. He looks out and down at the landscape. The November sun catches his face.
He pulls back. Looks around. He’s one of only a few passengers on the plane. He gets out of his seat.
John against the wall in the tight bathroom smoking a cigarette. A “No Smoking” placard displayed just next to him.
A group of destitute MEN line up at a MOBILE SOUP KITCHEN serving up hot soup and crackers and bottled water.
TRUDY KIERSTEAD, early 30’s, petite, short hair. Pious looking with a small cross around her neck. She spoons out soup from the big pot and into bowls for the men.
She offers faith-based words of encouragement to each man--

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: God praise. Lord be with you.
Trudy hands a bowl to the next man in line. A look of recognition on her face.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: Lord have mercy. Jesus loves you.
The man’s face goes unseen to us, as he sheepishly takes the bowl of soup, turns, and walks off.
Trudy watches after the man for a beat.
Out the plane’s window as the landing gear uncoils from under the wing and locks into place. In the distance lies the town of Dover, New Hampshire.
John shifts uncomfortably in his seat.
Small regional airport. A gathering of people crowd the arrival gate, waiting anxiously for their loved ones. Among them is Trudy.
She watches as passengers disembark the small jet. She checks her phone. Fixes her hair. Excited. Nervous.
She spots John step off the plane. She brightens, grows with excitement, as John crosses the tarmac and in through the arrival doors.
She waves at him. Their eyes lock. They smile. Trudy practically bursts through the crowd, throwing her arms around John. Big hug. Buries herself into him.
She holds on. Her smile slowly fades. John’s fades, too.
The luggage carousel. John waits for his baggage to arrive. Trudy stands next to him. She peeks up at her big brother, studying him without him noticing.
Trudy drives. John has his window rolled down. He looks out at the Dover sights and sounds. He grows agitated.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: He, um, well... we live together now.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: He moved in? Into the house?

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: Yeah. It’s serious now, John. You know? In a good way. A very good way. We’re still tryin’ for kids, but... Maybe it’s just not in God’s plan, right?

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: I think dad liked having another cop around. Someone to talk to. Cop stuff? You know?

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: The financial’s alone, John. I mean, we split everything fifty- fifty, and--
They drive in silence for a while. They cross the bridge that spans the Cocheco River and into downtown Dover. Suddenly, Trudy, like she just remembered something big--

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: Shit! You must be starving. Hey, let’s do Angelo’s!

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: You know, I can’t even remember the last time I had Angelo’s.
John in the car parked outside Angelo’s Pizza on Main Street. Trudy can be seen inside the pizza shop, ordering.
It’s around midday. On the street there’s a fair bit of activity. A few passing folks seem to recognize John.
Two TEEN BOYS on bikes pass by, slowly. They stop.
teen) Hey, I think that’s John Kierstead.

elements.speaker: TEEN BOY #1
elements.text: My dad told me he saw him throw a rock straight across Salmon Falls River. The big part.

elements.speaker: TEEN BOY #1
elements.text: Says he saw him do it. Launched it clear into the State of Maine.
John, feeling self-conscious, sinks a bit in his seat. The teens approach the car.
John, startled, turns to see framed in the driver window an OLDER MAN, 70’s, camo jacket, dirty Budweiser hat.

elements.speaker: OLDER MAN
elements.text: Yessir! I thought I recognized ya. I used to fish with your dad.
John draws a blank. And he also doesn’t give a shit.

elements.speaker: OLDER MAN
elements.text: But then again, everybody fished with Mackie.

elements.speaker: FRANK
elements.text: Sorry about your dad. Too soon. He was a great man. Helluva cop.
John just nods. He fires up smoke.

elements.speaker: FRANK
elements.text: Say, didja ever get back into playin’ ball at all?
John eyeballs a liquor store across the street. He gets out of the car.

elements.speaker: FRANK
elements.text: Well, that’s a damn shame, ain’t it? You had some arm! Padres were scouting you heavy, weren’t they?

elements.speaker: TEEN BOY #2
elements.text: Did you really throw a rock across Salmon Falls River?
Trudy exits Angelo’s, pizzas in her arms. Sees John.
John, ignoring everyone, crosses the street. He ducks into the liquor store.
An old clapboard two-storey home. Well-kept. Lights on inside. Trudy’s car in the driveway. A sign hangs from the mailbox in the driveway that reads: The Kiersteads.
John and Trudy at the table. Boxes of Angelo’s Pizza between them. Only a few slices remain.
Crowding John are more than a few empty beer bottles. He twists open a fresh one and drinks. Trudy sips on some wine.
They sit in silence like this for a while. The only sounds are the refrigerator running and the ticking of a wall clock somewhere in the b.g., until finally...
John, not really acknowledging that remark, looks around the kitchen.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: I have an appointment with dad’s estate lawyer. The funeral’s been paid for by the VA and the police union, but as far as the house, the cabin...

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: We can talk to the lawyer. Both of us. Together.
John shrugs. He drinks. Trudy wipes away a sudden tear.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: Three days ago he was sitting right where you’re sitting. In that chair. We just had a barbecue.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: He was fine. Everything was fine.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: He wasn’t fine. For years, Tru.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: But he was fine! He started running again. Him and Doug. They ran every day. He was taking up yoga.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: He made fun of people who did yoga. He hated that shit.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: Well, he was all for it. He bought a mat and a membership and... and--
She starts to cry. John gets up and goes over to his little sister. He hugs her, as she lets it all out.
We hear a church choir begin to sing the classic funeral hymn “Be Not Afraid”, as...

slugline: INT. KIERSTEAD HOME - JOHN’S BEDROOM - NIGHT

elements.text: John steps into a bedroom. His old room. Now a guest room. He looks around. It stopped being his room long ago.
John in bed, unable to sleep. The hymn continues. He finally gets out of bed.
John at a motel front desk, checking in.
John in the darkened motel room watching an L.A. Dodgers game on TV and drinking more beer.
Trudy, housecoat on, cup of coffee in hand, walks down the hallway. She pauses at John’s bedroom door. She lays an ear to it. Listens. She knocks.
Trudy opens the door. Sees the bed made and no John.
Blustery November day. A sprawling cemetery under a sharp blue sky. CLOSE UP of a HEADSTONE. Etched into the stone:
Pull back to a freshly-dug grave, and John, alone, in suit and tie, sitting in the grass next to his parents headstone.
He stares down into the cold pit that is his father’s grave.
Old red-brick Catholic church. A throng of mourners dressed in black file through the wide-open doors.
The church parking lot is packed with cars, spilling out into curbside parking on both sides of the road. We see the hearse parked nearby, along with a convoy of Dover police cruisers.
Full house. Family, friends, members of the community, as well as many from law enforcement and the military. As if all of New Hampshire showed up.
At the lectern, the priest delivers a tearful eulogy--

elements.speaker: PRIEST
elements.text: We are here today to pay our tribute and our respect to a great man of God, our brother, our hero...
The casket up front, flanked by two easels holding framed portraits of Mackie in both his U.S. Marine dress blues and the full dress uniform of the Dover Police Department.

elements.speaker: PRIEST
elements.text: It has been said, “The measure of a life is not in its duration but in its donation.” Mackie Kierstead lived by this axiom, and to its fullest.
Draped over the casket are the Mackie’s uniforms, decorated with bars and medals of exceptional service and bravery. This man was nothing less than a hero.

elements.speaker: PRIEST
elements.text: We are also here to seek and receive comfort from God, trusting that He will minister to our hearts, and provide us with the strength to walk with Him during these unclear times.
Trudy is among the mourners in the front row, red-eyed, and holding tight the hand of her boyfriend, DOUG, 30, also dressed in the full dress uniform of the Dover PD.

elements.speaker: PRIEST
elements.text: ... As Jesus said, “Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted”.
Trudy turns and scans the congregation, searching for John. He’s nowhere to be found.
But someone does catch her eye -- a man, 60’s, in a U.S. Marines uniform. He’s REGGIE. He’s in good shape for his age, but tightly wound.
Reggie senses Trudy. He meets her somber gaze. He gives her a curt nod, and then looks away.
John sits against the backside of his parent’s headstone. Eyes closed. Almost asleep. He stirs at the sound of the funeral procession rolling in.

elements.speaker: PRIEST
elements.text: ... And from the Philippians: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain...
John stands, sees the Dover Police escort rounding a hilly bend, and then the hearse...

elements.speaker: PRIEST
elements.text: ... For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better...
... And then a black Lincoln Town Car, its passenger window rolled down and framing Trudy’s face veiled in black lace.
The interment. The grieving crowd at the grave site as the priest says a prayer and sprinkles holy water onto the casket as it’s slowly lowered down into the grave.
John is next to Trudy, who stands next to Doug. Trudy dabs away a tear from her eye. She takes a hold of John’s hand, tightly, and doesn’t let go.
Many cars shoe-horned into the Kierstead’s driveway. Many more line both sides of the narrow residential street.

slugline: INT. KIERSTEAD HOME - LIVING ROOM - CONTINUOUS

elements.text: The mourners have all gathered, everyone a tad less grief- stricken as they drink and eat and swap memorable stories about the late, great Mackie Kierstead.
Doug is busily handing out fresh cans of beers. Trudy tours around with a tray of sandwiches and a pot of coffee.
John gets the door. It’s Reggie. Still in his Marines uniform. A paper bag bulges under one arm. He steps inside.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: Sorry I’m late, kid. Been all over town tryin’ to find a bottle.
From the bag Reggie pulls out a bottle of Irish whiskey -- Tullamore Dew. Holds it out to John.
John smiles. Reggie smiles back. John takes the bottle.
Reggie sits on top of the washing machine. John’s at the window looking absently down at the street. Both men are drinking the Tullamore and smoking cigarettes.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: A fine thing you’ve done. Coming back. I know things weren’t smooth as butter for you two.
John ignores that remark, still looking out the window at...
JOHN’S POV: a car parked at the end of the street. Early model HONDA hatchback. Idling. A dark figure of a WOMAN sits behind the wheel.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: Let me be the one to say that your father would’ve appreciated this. I know Trudy does.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: How are you holding up, Reg?

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: I miss the sonofabitch. But, shit, he had a good run. Mackie was quality. One of the good ones. A true titan.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: I’d do anything for your father. And he for me. I extend that to you now, John. You and Trudy. Anything you need, just say the word.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: You, uh, speak to the estate lawyer?
He returns to the window, the Honda. Reggie watches him.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: You know, uh, your dad and I spent a lotta time at the cabin. He used to talk about it sometimes, the property, you know?

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: If anything should ever happen. He
didn’t want it going to pot.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: Lotta upkeep involved, I don’t hafta tell you. Winterizing, drain valves and the plumbing and all that. And then there’s external. Needs a new roof. Painting--

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: No offense, but Douglas ain’t exactly what you’d call a handyman. I mean, the cabin’s probably gonna go to you anyway, right?
Suddenly, the laundry room door opens and it’s Trudy. Unimpressed.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: Hi, Reggie. John, we need more ice.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: And there’s a lot of people downstairs who’re waiting to see you. At least go say hello.
John crushes out his smoke on the window sill, takes another glimpse at that Honda in the street.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Yes. Fine. I’ll get the ice.
John exits. Just Trudy and Reggie now. Reggie gestures to the window where John had been so preoccupied.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: Hundred bucks says she never gets out of her car.
Reggie studies her a moment. He knocks back his drink, shrugs, hops off the washer, and walks out.

slugline: INT. KIERSTEAD HOME - LIVING ROOM - LATER

elements.text: John on the couch being spoken to by a couple of cop buddies of his dad’s whom he doesn’t even know, or can’t remember knowing.
John, baseball in hand, giving an elderly man and a little boy a quick tutorial on how to throw a curveball.
Trudy takes away empty plates from some guests. She looks across the room at John who’s seated alone off in a corner, baseball in his hand, cycling rapidly through pitch grips.
Trudy senses his mood. She moves to go to him, but then hesitates and decidedly walks away.

slugline: EXT. KIERSTEAD HOME - FRONT PORCH - DUSK

elements.text: John alone on the front porch. It’s dusk, and the street lamps up and down the road all turn on at once.
In the new light John spots the Honda again, now parked almost directly across from John. Silhouetted inside the car is the figure of the woman.
John straightens, squints at the woman. He begins a casual move for the stairs.
Suddenly, the car turns on, lurches forward with a quick squeal, and peels away. John watches as the car rounds the corner and disappears.
The porch door opens. Doug steps out.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: You, uh, want to be left alone or--

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: No, no. Have a seat. Wanna smoke?
Doug sits. John hands him a cigarette, lights it for him.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: It’s good to see you home.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Oh, well. Work is work. Keeping the peace. Boy, this opioid thing, though. Epidemic around here.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: I imagine they’re keeping you pretty busy out there in L.A., huh?

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Say... how many homicides you boys got out there this year? So far?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Dunno. You sort of lose track of those things after a while, Doug.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Right... Wow. L.A. Hey, what do think, uh, the chances are that I guy like me, a cop like me, could get onto the force out there?
John to Doug with a “Don’t quit your day job” look.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Yeah. Got our own problems here in
A moment. Both men smoke. They stare out at the empty street.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Speaking of, um, problems, if it’s all the same with you, I mean, if you’re up for it, I was thinking you could come down to the station in the morning and get started.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Well, I just assumed you’d wanna look over your dad’s progress. I arranged all his case notes for you.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Missing persons cases aren’t exactly a routine thing around here, and, well, Mackie was doing us a pretty huge solid helping out.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Consulting on the Holly Roberts case?

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Aw, shit. Jesus, John. I thought you knew. I’m sorry. I thought Trudy -- she was gonna--
Trudy cling wraps a bowl of food, sticks it in the fridge. She starts to load the dishwasher as John walks in and grabs a beer from the fridge. Both seem a bit edgy.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I’m going back to the motel. Then I’m flying to L.A. in the morning.
Trudy sighs, shakes her head. She starts stabbing cutlery into the cutlery holder.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: I noticed you skipped out on your own father’s funeral.
John drinks his beer, simmering. Trudy cools--

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: Look, I know you and dad didn’t see eye-to-eye on things toward the end, but, what would mom think?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Yes. I asked her this morning at the cemetery. Said she was fine with it.
Trudy shoves the load of cutlery into the dishwasher and slams the door shut.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: You know what else she said? “Hey, John, look after your little sister, okay? Because even though she’s all grown up, she can still act like a complete immature fucking cunt.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: No! You hey! When were you gonna tell me about Cheyenne’s girl?
Doug appears. Pauses. Trudy looks to Doug, then back to John. Her anger dampens. She has no answer.
John glowers. He turns and leaves. A moment. He comes back.
Trudy goes after John. Doug stops her.
The sound of the front door as it’s slammed shut.
John drives through empty, late-night Dover, passing by 1800’s textile mills, credit unions and a Dunkin’ Donuts.
Along a stretch of road that skirts the Cocheco River. He stops at a red light. Across the street is a marina and a boat landing. John considers it.
Summer. Wide open bay. Blue sky day. YOUNG JOHN (19), ANDY (19), and two teen girls, one of them YOUNG CHEYENNE (African- American, pretty) are on a sleek new motorboat.
There’s loud music and plenty of beers. Andy is at the helm, beer in hand, smoking a joint.
Young Cheyenne sits close to a shirtless Young John. He’s fit, tanned, healthy, and donning a University of Southern California baseball cap.

elements.speaker: YOUNG JOHN
elements.text: So, how’d you convince your dad to let you take the boat out, anyway?

elements.speaker: ANDY
elements.text: Easy. Said a future Hall of Famer wants to go for a rip. How could he say no?
Andy looks back at John and winks. John smiles, takes the praise well, enjoys it, even. Cheyenne looks to John and smiles at him proudly.

elements.speaker: ANDY
elements.text: When the Padres offer you that fat- ass signing bonus, promise me you’ll take me out on your giant new yacht, okay?
The other girl (17), gets out of her seat, beer in hand, and a bit tipsy.

elements.speaker: OTHER GIRL
elements.text: Andy, can I drive the boat now? I wanna drive the boat.

elements.speaker: ANDY
elements.text: First of all, it’s called ‘piloting’. You pilot a boat.

elements.speaker: OTHER GIRL
elements.text: So let me fly the boat, then.

elements.speaker: ANDY
elements.text: No. Captain Johnny, take over. I need to roll us another fatty.
John chugs his beer, gets up and goes and takes the helm. Andy sits and takes out a bag of weed and rolling papers.
Suddenly, out of nowhere, a pair of JET-SKIERS whizz past the boat. A little too close. Their wake rocks the boat.

elements.speaker: ANDY
elements.text: Hey, Johnny, watch those fuckin’ jet-ski douchebags.
John steadies the boat. Andy shouts at the jet-skiers--

elements.speaker: ANDY
elements.text: Fuck you, assholes! Why don’t ya get a real fuckin’ boat?!
Other Girl throws her middle finger in the air at the jet- skiers. The jet-skiers whip a quick return 180.

elements.speaker: ANDY
elements.text: Open her up, Johnny. Show ‘em what she’s got.
John thrusts the throttle forward. The motor growls like a beast and the boat lurches and takes off, causing Andy to drop the weed as Other Girl stumbls and falls. She laughs.
Young Cheyenne holds on tight, glances back at the fast- approaching jet-skiers. She turns to John.

elements.speaker: YOUNG CHEYENNE
elements.text: John? I think you should slow down.
The jet-skiers split up, flanking both sides of the boat, hemming it in.
Andy grabs a beer can out of the cooler. Unopened. He whips it as hard as he can at one of the jet-skiers.
The beercan rings off the jet-skier’s arm, causing him to recoil, sending the jet-ski into a hard, awkward skid.
John watches the injured jet-skier, unaware of the 2nd skier banking in quick toward the boat.
SCREAMS from the girls. Somebody yells “LOOKOUT!”. Everything goes black to the noise of a horrific collision.
HONK of a horn. John snaps to, green light. He glances to his rearview at the car waiting behind him. John drives on.
Through the windshield POV of John pulling into an apartment complex made up of older 3-story townhouse buildings.
He spots something of interest at the rear-most building. It’s the little Honda. He pulls up to it, stops.
He glances down at the parking stall number painted on the asphalt: 305.
John knocks on the door to 305. The door opens revealing CHEYENNE, now late-30’s, and wearing an apron smeared with chocolate icing. She gives John a small, forgiving smile.
They linger a moment in the doorway, holding each other’s gaze. Studying one another. Revisiting a storied history as their expressions do the remembering for them.
Cheyenne in the kitchen as she puts on a fresh pot of coffee. John’s in the living room. He hasn’t taken off his coat.
The townhouse has been cheaply, yet thoughtfully, decorated. Ikea meets Thrift Store -- the fake-it-till-you-make-it effort of a struggling single mother.
John looks in at the kitchen, spots on the counter a freshly- baked chocolate cake and a bowl of chocolate icing.

elements.speaker: CHEYENNE
elements.text: Look, I’m sorry about this afternoon...
John turns to studying the living room.
Off in the corner sits a Lazy Boy recliner and a small table holding a few framed PHOTOS of Holly. Empty box of tissues sits next to it. And a nondescript bottle of PILLS.

elements.speaker: CHEYENNE
elements.text: I thought I’d be able to see you, but...
Cheyenne enters the living room, coffees in hand.

elements.speaker: CHEYENNE
elements.text: I’m sorry about Mackie. You know he meant a lot to me. He meant a lot to a lot of people.
John picks up a Holly photo. A school photo. Recent. 5th Grade. He holds onto it, looks to Cheyenne.
Cheyenne sets down the coffees. She sits.

elements.speaker: CHEYENNE
elements.text: All she wanted for her birthday was a new hobbyhorse -- you know, those stuffed toy horses on sticks? All her friends have ‘em. It’s like the new thing. But she was always stuck using second hand horses her friends didn’t want. She wanted one she could call her own.
Cheyenne takes out her phone, shows John a photo of a hobbyhorse.

elements.speaker: CHEYENNE
elements.text: Custom made. Exactly what she wanted.

elements.speaker: CHEYENNE
elements.text: Supposed to be a surprise, but she’s such a sneak, she found it, robbed it right out of the trunk of my car. Her and her friends went down to the nature preserve with it... the day she went missing.

elements.speaker: CHEYENNE
elements.text: That’s the only thing of Holly’s the police ever found.
Cheyenne looks to him. She turns on a hopeful expression.

elements.speaker: CHEYENNE
elements.text: Trudy... she, um, she said you might be able to help? Mackie, he was--
John’s eyes go back to that cake in the kitchen.

elements.speaker: CHEYENNE
elements.text: I understand if you don’t want to
POV John: on the photo of Holly in his hand. He slides the photo out of its frame sleeve.
John’s rental car as it drives through Dover.
Parked in an empty parking lot at a local park. John behind the wheel. We hold on him, as the sound of a boat engine builds slowly...
A police boat as it motors toward the Dover coast and the marina. The once sunny summer day has now clouded over.
On board are Young John, Cheyenne, and Other Girl. All wrapped in thermal blankets and looking pale and in shock.
Andy is nowhere to be seen.
Up ahead, a Dover Police DIVE BOAT fast approaches. It speeds past us and toward the open waters. John looks over at the dive boat and the police officers in their diving suits.
A worried MACKIE KIERSTEAD (50) stands at the edge of the dock. He looks out at the police boat approaching the shore.
Behind Mackie sits his unmarked police cruiser and a waiting ambulance and EMS personnel.

slugline: INT. DOVER POLICE PRECINCT - EVIDENCE ROOM - DAY
location_time: DOVER POLICE PRECINCT - EVIDENCE ROOM - DAY

elements.text: Overlooking a table in an evidence room. Holly’s custom-made hobbyhorse sits bagged and tagged in the middle of the table.
The night stand. John sets a fresh bottle of whiskey down next to his BOARDING PASS to L.A. and a folded-up funeral program, Mackie’s portrait on the front looking up at us.
He places the Holly photo onto the night stand, gently. He plops down onto the bed. He lays back. He stares across at the Holly photo.

slugline: INT. DOVER POLICE PRECINCT - EVIDENCE ROOM - DAY
location_time: DOVER POLICE PRECINCT - EVIDENCE ROOM - DAY

elements.text: John at the evidence table looking down at Holly’s hobbyhorse.
The door opens behind him and Doug enters with a thick accordion folder under his arm. Doug sets the folder down next to the hobbyhorse.
A moment. John glances over at the folder.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: You can sign it out before you leave.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Just let us know if you need anything else.
John nods. He returns to the hobbyhorse. Doug exits.
John digs out his phone. He takes some photos of the bagged hobbyhorse.
He snaps on a pair of latex gloves, and opens the bag. He lifts out the hobbyhorse. Examines it. Takes more photos.
Trudy sits with an estate lawyer as she signs off on a flurry of legal documents. The lawyer slides the keys and deed to the cabin into a large envelope labelled “John”.
A clerk’s desk. John signs off on his father’s case files.
John walks the precinct hallway, passing the Dover PD Wall of Fame -- portraits of past police chiefs and exceptional service men and women.
At the end of the hall, a maintenance worker affixes a framed portrait of Mackie to the wall. John passes by the tribute, barely acknowledging it.
A hard rain falls on Dover, as Young John stares out the window at Cheyenne being led into the back of an ambulance.
Mackie approaches us. He opens the door and gets in and shuts the door. He looks to his son, then out at the marina, at Cheyenne and the ambulance. His expression unreadable.

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: They’re gonna ask you some questions.
Young John nods. Mackie looks to his son.

elements.speaker: YOUNG JOHN
elements.text: They came at us, dad. We were just... I ran out of room.

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: They failed the Breathalyzer. Whatever they say happened won’t matter anyway.

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: But Andy shouldn’t have been drinking.

elements.speaker: YOUNG JOHN
elements.text: We were all drinking. And, Dad, I was the one who was--

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: Wouldn’t have happened had he been sober. He took his father’s boat without asking and--

elements.speaker: YOUNG JOHN
elements.text: His dad let him use the boat.

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: Operating a watercraft while under the influence.

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: He put everyone’s safety in danger.

elements.speaker: YOUNG JOHN
elements.text: Dad, I told you I was the one--
KNOCKS on Mackie’s window. It’s a DOVER COP in a rain poncho.
Mackie rolls down his the window.
Cop looks at John, then at Mackie.

elements.speaker: DOVER COP
elements.text: Dive team made a recovery... Positive I.D.
Mackie nods, rolls up the window as the Cop walks away.

elements.speaker: YOUNG JOHN
elements.text: We don’t have to do this.

elements.speaker: YOUNG JOHN
elements.text: Dad, it’s okay. I’ll say it was me. The jet skiers. I panicked--

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: John! You fucked up. You can’t undo this. You want to ruin two lives now?

elements.speaker: YOUNG JOHN
elements.text: You’re not putting this on Andy.

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: Got that? Now, listen to me--

elements.speaker: YOUNG JOHN
elements.text: But I was the one. Don’t put it on him.

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: Listen to me, John! Are you out of your fucking mind?! You guys crossed state lines. Did you know that?
John’s look: clearly he was not aware.

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: Maine State Police are gonna jump all over this. They’re gonna wanna know what happened on their watch.

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: You tell ‘em whatever the hell you want. But remember, as soon as you talk, I can’t protect you.
Mackie starts the car. Puts it in gear.

elements.speaker: MACKIE
elements.text: Besides, you got baseball coming up.
Mackie, all business, drives on. John sits stunned.

slugline: EXT. APARTMENT BALCONY - RESEDA, CALIFORNIA - DAY

elements.text: A not-too-shabby apartment complex in sunny Reseda. Angie the hooker sits on her balcony in a skimpy 2-piece, drinking beer and painting her toenails a bright blue. Her phone rings.
John zips his suitcase shut. He’s checking-out.
John pockets his boarding pass from off the night stand.

elements.speaker: ANGIE
elements.text: Well, where you at? I’ll swing by.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Ang... how does a person know if they’re doing the right thing?

elements.speaker: ANGIE
elements.text: Just come back home where you belong, baby. A’ight? I'll fuck your brains out. On the house.
Road sign: Airport exit. John drives past it.
John’s rental parked in the Kierstead driveway.

elements.speaker: ANGIE
elements.text: Man, I don’t know. Ya just... I guess ya just feel something?
John enters the kitchen. Sees his envelope from the estate lawyer sitting on the table. He sets down his luggage.

elements.speaker: ANGIE
elements.text: I haven’t always done the right thing. Duh. But, ya know, whether right or wrong, John, we all got a voice in our head...
John goes to the envelope. He opens it.

elements.speaker: ANGIE
elements.text: It’ll never tell ya what to do. But it’ll always tell ya what NOT to do.
Trudy in the backyard vegetable garden, toiling away, harvesting the last of this autumn’s crop -- pumpkin, squash, corn.

elements.speaker: ANGIE
elements.text: I guess ya gotta listen for that, ya know?
Trudy hears the back door swing open. She turns and sees John standing there, twirling the cabin keys on his finger. She puts down her garden tools and goes to John. She hugs him.
Eggs and bacon sizzle on a frying pan on the Kierstead stove.
John and Doug are seated at the table. Doug’s in his police uniform, wolfing down his breakfast. John has barely touched his plate, his side of the table covered with case reports and police photos.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Uh, the warden at the nature preserve. Holly’s father Pete. Cheyenne, of course. It's all in Mackie’s reports.
Trudy at the stove, glances to John.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: I was thinking: why don’t we all go to the cabin this weekend? Catch the fall colors before they’re gone?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Reggie says the place needs work.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Cheyenne mentioned Holly was with some friends the day she went missing.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Right. Mackie talked to them. There should be a transcript of it in there.
Doug reaches across with greasy fingers, grabs a handful of papers and sifts through them for the transcripts.

elements.speaker: TRUDY
elements.text: You know Reggie’s been trying to get dad to sell him the cabin. Don’t be surprised if he asks you.
He hands John a single page. John takes it, scans it.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Where’s the rest? This is a blurb, barely half a page.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: This is it. I mean... the girls, they were pretty shook up when I questioned them the night Holly disappeared. Apparently still shook up when Mackie talked to them.
John’s POV: 8 X 10 photo of Holly’s hobbyhorse.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Those girls are the last people to have seen Holly alive. They need to be questioned again.
Trudy comes over with the skillet of eggs, bacon. She serves a heap of it onto John’s plate. It goes unnoticed by John who’s now hyper-focused on the hobbyhorse photo.
He draws closer to the photo, squints at it. Trudy goes to refill John’s glass of OJ. He puts his hand over his glass.
John with the photo springs out of his seat and leaves the kitchen.

slugline: INT. MACKIE’S DEN - KIERSTEAD HOME - MOMENTS LATER
location_time: MACKIE’S DEN - KIERSTEAD HOME - MOMENTS LATER

elements.text: A table laid out with fly-tying hobby equipment. A magnifying lamp sits clamped to the table. John and Doug both peer through the magnifying lens.
ANGLE ON: the magnifying lamp. The hobbyhorse photo is slipped behind the lens. The image zooms up at us.
Words branded into the wooden stick of the hobbyhorse read:

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Cheyenne said she had it custom made...
John looks to Doug who shrugs and shakes his head “no”.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Never heard of it. I think it’s an angle your dad never thought of, though.
John’s look says he isn’t entirely convinced.
John’s car. Mackie’s case files rest on the dash. Through the windshield we see people filing in and out of a local hockey arena -- young girls, parents and spectators.
Beth and Krista are seen entering the arena, hobbyhorses poking out of gym bags slung over their shoulders.
A show jumping course has been set up on the arena floor. Girls with hobbyhorses run the course and perform dressage. Judges mark and score their rounds.
ARENA SEATS John and Beth and Krista sit in the stands. Both girls seem not in the best of spirits.

elements.speaker: BETH
elements.text: I don't get why we gotta talk about this stuff over and over. Don't you cops share notes?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I'm sorry that you have to answer all these questions. I know that the past week has been very rough. For the both of you.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I know. I do, too. Now, is there anything else you can remember -- about that day? The day before? The week before? Anything?

elements.speaker: BETH
elements.text: We said no. What else are we supposed to say? We don’t know what she did 24 hours a day. We don’t know what her thoughts were. How am I supposed to know where she rides her bike when I’m not around, or what emails she gets, or who some random she was texting all the time was?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Was she texting someone? A stranger?
Beth, big sigh. She gives up. Krista chimes in--

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Was it a boy? Someone she went to school with maybe?
An announcer over the PA calls the next competitors.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Why didn’t you tell this to Detective Kierstead when he interviewed you?
Announcer calls Beth and Krista. Beth gets out of her seat. She flashes John a snarky look--
She heads down to the competition floor. Krista lingers a moment, awkwardly, then gets up and follows Beth. She stops and turns to John.

elements.speaker: KRISTA
elements.text: Holly was always nice to me. I really hope you find her.
She turns back and heads off down to the arena floor.
A waterfront fish and chips truck. Doug and John walk away from it carrying darkly-greased take-out bags. John opens his bag, peeks into it. He winces.
He pulls out of the bag a skimpy piece of battered cod. It’s mostly batter.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: You know, I expect this in L.A., but here...
Doug shrugs. He tosses a fistful of fries into his mouth.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: I read in the paper... seventy percent of our seafood is exported...

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: To New York. If ya can believe it.
They arrive at Doug’s police cruiser. John sets down his food, bothered by something else besides the fish.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I don’t understand. Why would he leave something like that out?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: And the dates. Timelines. Says he spoke to the girls Monday, but it was really Sunday.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: John. Don’t take this the wrong way or anything, but you haven’t been around. Mackie was in rough shape. I mean, who knows? Maybe his memory was fading.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: No. He’s a better cop than that.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: It’s like he knew that somebody would be reading his notes... somebody he didn’t want reading them.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Don’t look into it like that. We got a lead. That’s enough for me.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: It’s a bullshit report, man. And you know it.
Doug takes the insult on behalf of himself and Mackie. He checks his watch.
John looks down at his seafood. Picks through the fries for any morsels of actual fish. He gives up.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Holly? We did that. It’s dead.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Do it again. Call her provider, bring up her records, see who she was texting.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: As far as you can get.
On the ferry. John emerges from his car. He lights a cigarette and heads over to the ferry’s edge.
It’s overcast with a cold, bitter wind. John pops his collar to shield the bite. He draws his coat in for warmth. A world away from sunny Los Angeles.
He casts his gaze out across the bay, to the island still far off but drawing nearer with every passing moment.
The island: Desolate. Rugged. Almost ominous, shaded darkly by dense pines and firs that push to the extreme edges of the shoreline -- as if the trees themselves are desperate to escape something.
Old island road. Barely maintained. John’s rental appears from around the bend, passing by us.
POV: through the windshield as John idles at a private side road blocked by a low-hung chain strung across its entrance.
We stay here as John gets out and goes to the chain, unlocks one end with his cabin keys, and lets the chain fall.
He comes back to the car and gets in, and then we drive off down the private dirt road a ways until John suddenly has to hit the brakes for--
A pick-up truck blocking the road. It’s Reggie’s truck.
A U.S. Marines decal in the back window. A rifle rack hangs above it, clutching a 12 gauge shotgun with a scope.
John walks up. Checks out Reggie’s truck. He then walks on down the dirt road.
John exits the road and into a grassy clearing and the cabin on the other side. It’s a white clapboard A-frame, old and small but well-maintained.
The whine of a power saw is heard from somewhere on the other side of the cabin.
A half-built patio sits over an old root cellar.
He’s bent over a plank of wood, cutting through it with the power saw. He senses something. He stops his cut. The saw powers down. He straightens, turns. Smiles.
We see John standing here, cabin keys dangling from his finger.
The kitchen. Cozy. Rustic. Reggie rummages in the fridge.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: Had I’d known you were coming...
He comes up with two beers.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: ... I’d have brought along a few more beers.
He hands a bottle to John, who takes it.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: And had I’d known you were coming...
Reggie pauses. An almost sheepish smile as he twists open his beer and flicks the bottle cap into the sink.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: Yeah. Heard the place is all yours now. Congrats.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: The patio was one of our projects. I thought it’d be fitting to see it through.
John wanders off into the living room. Reggie follows.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: So, uh, what brings you out here today, anyway?
Lived in. Cluttered with take-out containers and empty beer cans. Dirty laundry lay strewn across the floor and around the pull-out couch. Clearly Reggie’s been sleeping here.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: It’s been twenty years since I stepped foot in here.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: When you and Trudy were kids, you used to come out here, those hot fuckin’ summers, remember? You’d be out back practicing your pitches.
John turns his gaze to the fireplace mantle that holds a few framed photos. He walks over to it.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: Poor Trudy, you’d force her to swing that old bat over and over. Remember that?
One of the photos is of a younger John (10), beaming, holding up a modest looking trout. Fresh catch.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: After a few swings it was like she was trying to lift a tree trunk, she was so exhausted.
John lifts up the photo, looks at it closely.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: But you were good, John. Real good.
John sets the photo back onto the mantle.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Reggie? Where were you the day Holly Roberts disappeared?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I’ve agreed to look into the case.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: Is that why you’re here? To question me?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Nah. Just procedure. I couldn’t find any record of PD or my dad ever speaking to you. Thought I’d just dot that “i”.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: C’mon, John. Least stay in the damn strike zone, will ya?

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: Look, if I were you, I’d be taking a hard look at that hombre Cheyenne’s been rolling with.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: And which hombre would that be?

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: Gang-banger. From Boston. Yeah. He drives around in some gaudy Chrysler 300. Doug didn’t tell ya?
John seems disturbed by this. He swigs his beer. He heads back into the kitchen.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: It’s them fuckin’ opiates, you know. They’re here.
John puts on his coat. Reggie enters.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: And Cheyenne... She’s gone got herself all mixed up in it. Deep.

elements.speaker: REGGIE
elements.text: Oh, but it does. This is my town. This was Mackie’s town. It’s still your town, too, John.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I’m just doing a favor. That’s it.
He’s almost out the door, stops, comes back.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: My father ever speak privately to you about the Holly Roberts case?
John thinks for a moment. Nods. He turns and leaves. That’s it. No further questions.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Make sure you lock up when you’re done.
Reggie takes a slug of beer and watches John through the window walk across the clearing back toward the road.
The townhouses. A hard November rain pummels everything. In a far corner of the parking lot sits John’s car.
John in his car. Radio tuned to AM sports talk. Baseball. Red Sox off-season and the upcoming college draft.
John sips on a cup of coffee, Dunkin’ Donuts. He hits the wipers to refresh his view of Cheyenne’s townhouse building.
Cheyenne emerges from her townhouse in a waitress uniform. She looks a bit strung out. She pauses under the entrance way overhang and lights a cigarette. She hops on her phone.
John with an eye on Cheyenne. Over the AM radio--

elements.speaker: RADIO HOST
elements.text: College pitching is a strength in this year’s draft. Our righty out of Florida, Emerson Spencer, will likely go #1. Deep toolbox of pitches, an ability to pound the strike zone, and a 98-mph fastball, the kid’s a stud-force. Absolute savage.
CLICK. John’s shuts the radio off. He flips the hood up on his coat and zips up and goes to exit the car, but then...
A DEEP ROLLING NOISE. Lots of rhythm and bass. John checks his rearview: a pair of headlights from a car slowly approaches through the rain.
The car gets closer, the noise growing louder. John’s windows begin to vibrate from the soundwaves.
It’s gangsta rap. As the car passes, John can see clearly it’s a Chrysler 300, black and with Massachusetts plates. It pulls up to Cheyenne. She hops in and the 300 drives off.
John in traffic tailing the 300. The rain has switched over to sleet making for slower than usual traffic.
Intersection. Red light. Everyone slows to a stop, as John creeps over into the adjacent lane alongside the 300 passenger side.
Inside, sits Cheyenne. She raps along to the music, cigarette in her hand. John peeks past and over at the driver: he’s Hispanic, 30’s, hoodie and a Boston Celtics ball cap.
Cheyenne senses eyes on her. She glances over and does a double-take as she meets John’s gaze. She stops rapping.
The two of them hold a look. Cheyenne looks away first.
John’s phone rings. Without taking his eyes off Cheyenne, he answers--
Doug at his desk, looking at his computer screen.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Mostly text messages to friends. And Cheyenne.
Green light. Traffic moves. John falls back and switches lanes again to stay behind the 300.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: But there’s this other number. No longer in service. T-Mobile says it was probably one of them Wal-Mart burner-phone dealies? So I tracked the tower pings, and the last call made on that number was the morning

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: John, you can’t just go and--

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I need you to run a plate. Ready?
The 300 pulls over to a Denny’s restaurant. John pulls over.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Listen to me, John -- don’t go to Biddeford.
Cheyenne hops out of the 300 and rushes into the Denny’s.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Yes. I got it. But, look...
Doug glances around the office, leans into his phone.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: You’re already way out of your jurisdiction. So promise me that you won’t go--
Close up of wood being cut by a power saw. Shots of workers sanding, hammering, operating machinery. More than a few workers are visibly mentally disabled.

slugline: INT. LAND & SEA WOODWORKS - FRONT OFFICE - DAY
location_time: LAND & SEA WOODWORKS - FRONT OFFICE - DAY

elements.text: John in business casual attire talking with the receptionist. From the shop floor enters a MANAGEMENT type, 50’s. He greets John.

elements.speaker: MANAGEMENT
elements.text: Mr. Matthews, thank you for coming.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Thanks for having me on such short notice.
Management motions to the shop floor door.
Management giving John a tour of the noisy shop floor--

elements.speaker: MANAGEMENT
elements.text: We run mainly a production line of furniture and cabinetry, with a few custom lines here and there.
More shots of workers busily assembling wood products at various stages of completion.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: How many workers do you employ?

elements.speaker: MANAGEMENT
elements.text: Depends on the size of the run. 20 to 30 on average. We’re also unique in that our workforce is an integrated workforce, consisting of, as you can see, folks with and without disabilities.
We focus on one young Hispanic man, 20’s, operating a lathe machine. He clearly is not one of the disabled.

elements.speaker: MANAGEMENT
elements.text: Last year was a particularly good sales year. 3 million in revenue stream, a large chunk of which we funnel back into services and programs for the disabled.
The young Hispanic takes notice of the two men, showing particular concern towards John.

elements.speaker: MANAGEMENT
elements.text: You mentioned your company’s interested in our premium line of custom hobbyhorses?
John scans the faces of the workers, lands on the Hispanic. He and John trade a look.
The Hispanic returns to his work.
Management leads John to an office just off the shop floor.
Management hands John some sales brochures, motions John to have a seat.
John sits, positioning himself with a view through the office window and the young Latino at his lathe machine.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: My company. We are very excited to branch out into the toy and hobby market.

elements.speaker: MANAGEMENT
elements.text: Well, we run a couple hobbyhorse lines. One in late spring, the other closer to the Christmas season.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Now, do you assign certain skilled workers to those lines?

elements.speaker: MANAGEMENT
elements.text: Yes, we do, actually. The horses are all hand-made, custom painted, air-brushed.

elements.speaker: MANAGEMENT
elements.text: We cut our own leather for the bridles. It’s a specialty line that we here at land and sea take particular pride in.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Is it at all possible if I could meet the hobbyhorse makers?

elements.speaker: MANAGEMENT
elements.text: Matter of fact, we got one of our makers on the floor right now. Let me call him in.
Management picks up his office phone, hits the PA button.

elements.speaker: MANAGEMENT
elements.text: Ricardo. Come to my office, please.
RICARDO freezes. He looks over at the office and spots John in the window staring out at him with a dubious look.
Ricardo shuts off his machine. He takes his time removing his protective eye wear, his gloves, and his ear plugs.
John POV: as Ricardo leaves his station and begins to walk toward us...
Suddenly, he takes an abrupt turn and heads briskly down a hallway.
John bolts across the shop toward the hallway where Ricardo disappeared. A woman carrying an arm-load of wood appears. John doesn’t stop, bumps her hard but keeps running.
The wood and the woman spill to the floor. Co-workers quickly come to her aid. We see she clearly has Down’s Syndrome. She is deeply shocked and very upset at being hit.
John sprints the hallway just as the exit door at the end swings shut. He reaches the door, shoulders through it, and bursts out into...
Lumber yard. The shock of freezing rain. John spots Ricardo fleeing toward a chain-link fence at the opposite end of the yard. John sprints after him.
A sloping pile of rough-hewn lumber stacked against the fence. Ricardo hits it, climbs up, and leaps over the fence, dropping into...
A storage lot filled with rows of parked tractor trailers. Ricardo cuts between trailers and disappears from sight.
John gets to the fence, bounds up the wood pile. The wood is slick with frozen rain. He loses his footing and stumbles hard onto the cold heavy lumber.
He gets up and keeps going, wincing as he gingerly climbs the fence and drops into the storage lot.
John moves slowly between two trailers, stopping at the end to peer around the corners. He moves ahead down another corridor of trailers.
He pauses. Listens. Tough to hear anything over the sharp sound of sleet cutting against the metal of the trailers.
Shit. Muscle memory. He never did bring his gun from L.A.
Then a dull THUD from above. John looks up and glimpes Ricardo on the roof of a nearby trailer.
Ricardo leaps off and onto another trailer roof. The race is on. Ricardo above and John below. John makes a shortcut diagonally between rows, trying to keep up with Ricardo.
John stops between trailers. He’s lost sight of Ricardo. Checks out the corners. He peeks underneath. Nothing.
Suddenly, a dark shape soars above between the trailers. Then a thud as Ricardo lands on the roof.
A metal ladder bolted to the trailer end. John climbs it.
John appears at the edge and catches Ricardo making another leap over onto one more trailer up ahead.
John climbs onto the roof, swallows his nerves and breaks into a run to the other end... LEAPS the gap onto...
John lands. Ricardo watches from the other end. They exchange a look, then Ricardo turns and leaps off onto the ground.
John sprints to the end, makes a leap of faith off the trailer. Soars. Committed. Then arms flailing until his fall is broken as he pounces hard onto Ricardo.
Both men crash to the muddy half-frozen dirt of the lot. John to his knees. Ricardo lies there. Wind knocked out of him. He groans.
John stands, out of breath, adrenalin pumping. He smiles--
He yanks Ricardo to his feet.
We move over a bare, leafless forest -- dozens of search team volunteers in bright orange vests fan out across the forest floor.
A missing persons poster of Holly stapled to a telephone pole. Half the poster is encrusted with sleet, the other half barely hanging on, whipped by the gusty winds.
John paces outside a door in a secluded alcove sectioned off from the rest of the precinct.
The door opens and Doug comes out of a room that certainly isn’t any official interrogation room. He looks around, worried. John goes to him, expectant:

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Why did you have to bring him here?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: What? We supposed to grill the guy in some back alley? Tell me what he said.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: I didn’t get much out of him. Except he thought you were ICE.
Doug produces a Social Security card. John takes it, looks it over.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Says he bought it off the street down in Boston.
John sits down across from Ricardo, who’s cut-up and exhausted from the foot chase. Doug’s here, too, standing at the door, keeping a close eye out the door’s little window.
***the preceeding exchange will be spoken in Spanish with English subtitles**

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: How long you been working there?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: You like it here? You like America? You can support your kids with that pay check?
Oh, that’s right, you don’t have any kids. You’re here all alone. You’re a loner. Guess what?
John slaps the fake Social Security card onto the table.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: That card is fraudulent. That makes you a fraud. Now, I’m calling ICE unless you tell me what you know.

elements.speaker: RICARDO
elements.text: I know nothing. I swear. I just work. I love America.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Who else? Who’s on your team?

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Who makes the fucking hobbyhorses, Ricardo?! Who else?!
Doug shifts uncomfortably, concerned at John’s temper. He takes a quick peek out the door window.
John stares down Ricardo, waiting. Finally...

elements.speaker: RICARDO
elements.text: Two other men. Alberto Gomez and Raymond Olsen.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Alberto and Raymond. Okay. Good. More. Tell me more.

elements.speaker: RICARDO
elements.text: Raymond no longer works with us. They fired him a month ago.

elements.speaker: RICARDO
elements.text: I still see him at the bar.
Doug hears the name, perks up. John looks over at him.

elements.speaker: DOUG
elements.text: Remember O’Leary’s Pub? Across from the Legion?
John nods. He turns back to Ricardo.

elements.speaker: RICARDO
elements.text: Alberto lives in Dover. We all used to go the bar every Friday night after work. He’s a very good friend of mine.

elements.speaker: RICARDO
elements.text: He hasn’t been to work in a week. I check his apartment. He not there either. I think ICE get him. That’s why I run from you.
John leans back in his chair, puzzled, trying to fit the pieces together. Suddenly--
John turns, sees Doug backing away from the door as it swings open and CAPTAIN MARCHAND enters.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: Take his statement and cut him loose.
John sighs, stands, and goes with the Captain.
The Captain sits at his desk. He shakes his head at John who sits in front of him.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: I can’t believe I’m saying this -- You are not a member of this police force.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: Yes, sir. I understand that, sir.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: You are not a member of Homeland Security. Or Immigration. You’re certainly not FBI.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: You are an outside agent acting in a consultancy role with the Dover Police Department on an active missing persons investigation. You review the available information that we provide, and in turn give your educated opinion to us based on the facts at hand.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: Then do you care to tell me why you’ve been running all over New England playing a bad Dick Tracy?

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: Arresting innocent individuals, dragging them across state lines, and accusing them of--

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I didn’t arrest him. I detained him. And he’s an illegal.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: I don’t give a shit! Now look--

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: All due respect, sir, my father’s files on Holly Roberts--

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: Do not interrupt me! Don’t do that.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: I’ve received two upsetting phone calls today.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: One from Maine State Police who say they received a phone call from a local business owner who’s filed an official complaint about a cop impersonating a salesman scaring the hell out of all of his employees.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: I got a second call from Mr. Reginald Lund. Reggie says you’ve been throwing malicious accusations around that he might be somehow wrapped up in this whole thing.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: I request permission to take lead investigative role.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: Permission fucking denied. You got twenty four hours to file a report.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: It’s been a week. We both know the grim stats on kids missing beyond a week.

elements.speaker: JOHN
elements.text: You can’t -- Why would you? There’s no known interstate transportation -- if you just let me, sir, give me some more time--

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: She is a girl of tender years, 12 and under -- they can monitor interstate travel -- they’ll share with us intel on other kidnapping situations --

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: You had your time, John. No way.
Your job is done here. Understood?
A commotion outside the door. Shouting. It grows closer. Captain goes to his door, opens it.
Just down the hall officers try to keep back an irate man, 40’s, who is shouting, looking into offices.

elements.speaker: IRATE MAN
elements.text: Kierstead! Kierstead, that fuck! I wanna see him!
An officer rushes to the Captain--
John appears. He heads to the irate man, PETE (30’s).
Pete spots John, b-lines for him as officers try to grab him but he just keeps coming. Even Captain intervenes. But its too late -- POP!
Pete gets one solid punch into John’s face before the dog pile begins. John stumbles from the punch. He collapses to the floor, holding his jaw.
Doug and Pete and the Captain. Pete’s handcuffed, his face showing the effects of what happens when you punch a cop in front of a bunch of other cops.
John walks in the room holding an ice pack over his jaw. Pete glances at him.

elements.speaker: PETE
elements.text: I never met the guy in person, okay? How was I supposed to know there’s two detective Kierstead’s in the same fuckin’ town?

elements.speaker: PETE
elements.text: Is anybody on this police force actually working this case? I mean, what the hell is going on up here? Nobody returns my calls. You won’t even gimmie an update--

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: Pete. We’re doing our best. But you have to understand that this is still an active investigation. We simply cannot release info prematurely to--
Doug steps over and uncuffs Pete.

elements.speaker: CAPTAIN MARCHAND
elements.text: Now, Pete. Tell Detective Kierstead what you just told us, and what you told the other Detective Kierstead.
Captain nods. John tosses his lighter and his pack of smokes onto the table. Pete lights one, smokes, and goes on--

elements.speaker: PETE
